newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba bangs drum for stable, credible Euro.
newsitem.headline: Buba bangs drum for stable, credible Euro.

text.p: The German Bundesbank, one of the most powerful voices in the shaping of Europe's single currency, on Tuesday forged ahead in its campaign to make sure that the new Euro will be stable and credible from the start.

Franz-Christoph Zeitler, a Bundesbank council member and head of the Bavarian regional central bank, made clear in a speech to a business congress that countries wishing to join monetary union must meet the entry criteria in a credible way.

While welcoming the idea of a so-called stability pact to enforce fiscal discipline within monetary union, Zeitler made clear that this was not an excuse to be lax when evaluating countries' efforts to meet budgetary goals next year.
"Even a stability pact should not deflect from a clear and credible fulfilment of budgetary criteria in particular at entry to the currency union," he said, speaking in Italy.

Separately, Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, head of the Berlin regional central bank, said EMU should start on time in 1999 with a small group of nations rather than risk delaying the project or softening the criteria to let more nations in.

"There should certainly not be an automatism as far as the timing for the start of monetary union if this has a softening of the criteria as precondition," he said. "It would therefore be sensible to start with a small group".

The comments are the most recent in a series of Bundesbank comments poking a critical finger at some countries attempts to bend the rules as far as they can to squeeze their 1997 budget deficits to match the standard set for EMU.

According to the terms of the Maastricht Treaty, countries which want to meld their currencies in the Euro must meet strict economic goals on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public borrowing in 1997.

With most core countries pretty much on target for the first three criteria, it is the budgetary guidelines which have drawn the spotlight, particularly as countries come up with increasingly creative ways of improving their 1997 budget figures by including one-off income or deferring payments.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer lashed out at such practices in a speech on Monday, making clear that it was not sufficient to reach a one-time target in 1997, adding that countries must demonstrate fiscal dicipline long-term.
In a very forthright statement of his views, Tietmeyer fell short only of naming the names of those countries that may be taking a less than purist approach to their national accounts.

When asked to comment directly in recent weeks on action taken by Germany's closest European ally, France, to include one-off revenues in its 1997 budget figures, Tietmeyer and Finance Minister Theo Waigel have simply said that the European Commission must decide whether such tactics are permissable.

In his speech on Tuesday, Zeitler also stressed the need for fiscal consolidation to show long-term, and not one-off, results. It was not enough to simply set up a stability pact as a safety net to catch budgetary offenders, he said.

Likening the EMU project to a any commercial design project, Zeitler said: "Even in the case of a technical construction no one would even suggest running functionality tests more laxly before it first started operating properly, on the grounds that the equipment would be serviced continually."

Aware of the sensitivity of financial markets to comments on European monetary union and statements from the Bundesbank itself, Zeitler warned cautiously in his speech that markets must not be allowed to grow worried about the Euro's stability.
The consequence of such worries could be a flight of capital out of the "hard-core" European countries -- those which most closely meet the Maastricht criteria -- he warned.
